Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Review the epidemiology of, etiology of, and risk factors for diabetes mellitus.
Review the management of hyperglycemia.
Describe the complications of diabetes mellitus.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Common group of diseases characterized by hyperglycemia from insulin insufficiency
Two main subsets: type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus
Type 1 diabetes mellitus: hyperglycemia from insulin deficiency secondary to destruction of
pancreatic beta cells




NOTES

1/21

Also known as insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus or juvenile diabetes mellitus; however,
these terms currently are used less commonly because they may be misleading.
Type 2 diabetes mellitus: hyperglycemia from insulin resistance
Previously known as noninsulin-dependent diabetes mellitus or adult-onset diabetes
mellitus

Overview
Diabetes mellitus is a group of common diseases characterized by hyperglycemia from
insulin insufficiency. Prediabetes mellitus results in impaired glucose tolerance, and
patients with the condition are at risk for diabetes mellitus. The two main subsets of
diabetes mellitus are type I and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Type 1 diabetes mellitus is less
common and is caused by insulin deficiency secondary to destruction of pancreatic beta
cells. Type 2 diabetes mellitus, which is more common, is caused by insulin resistance.
Initially it is characterized by elevated insulin levels but eventually may progress to
inability to secrete insulin (Figure 1).
Patients with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus have chronic hyperglycemia, which
damages organ systems and frequently affects the eyes, nerves, and kidneys and
cardiovascular and musculoskeletal systems.

Figure 1 Illustrations show normal physiology compared with type 1 and type 2 diabetes
mellitus. (Adapted with permission from Phair K: Managing Diabetes the Nice Way
[webinar]. Roseville, MN, Nice Healthcare, May 13, 2021. Available at:
https://www.nice.healthcare/the-nicessities/managing-diabetes-webinar. Accessed
July 18, 2022.)
Epidemiology
13% of American adults have diabetes mellitus.
Diabetes mellitus is one of the top 10 leading causes of death in the United States.
More than 20% of patients with diabetes mellitus are unaware of their condition.
The prevalence is highest among American Indians, Hispanics, and Blacks.
The prevalence varies considerably by education and socioeconomic status.

Epidemiology
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimate that 34.5% of US adults have
prediabetes mellitus (hemoglobin A1c level of 5.7% to 6.4%), and 13% of American adults
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:50 AM
AAOS | Diabetes Mellitus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003007
3/21

have diabetes mellitus, with 1.5 million new cases of diabetes mellitus diagnosed
annually in adults. Type 1 diabetes mellitus accounts for approximately 5% of diabetes
mellitus cases. The prevalence of diabetes mellitus (type 1 and type 2) is increasing
considerably.1 The rapid increase in the number of individuals with type 2 diabetes
mellitus is tied closely to increases in obesity and sedentary lifestyle. The increase in
diagnoses is particularly concerning because diabetes mellitus is among the top 10
leading causes of death in the United States, and more than 20% of patients with
diabetes mellitus are unaware of their condition.1
Prevalence varies considerably by education and socioeconomic status: more cases are
diagnosed among adults with less than a high school education compared with those
who graduated high school. In addition, the prevalence is highest among American
Indians, Hispanics, and Blacks.1
Anatomy and Physiology
Insulin promotes glucose absorption from the blood into liver, fat, and skeletal muscle.
Insulin is produced and secreted by pancreatic beta cells, which are located in the islets of
Langerhans.

Anatomy and Physiology
The hormone insulin regulates the amount of glucose in the bloodstream by managing
glucose absorption and storage. It is produced and secreted by pancreatic beta cells. The
islets of Langerhans, scattered throughout the parenchyma, contain the endocrine cells
of the pancreas. In addition to insulin, the islets produce glucagon (insulin’s
counterregulatory hormone), somatostatin, C-peptide, amylin, pancreatic polypeptide,
and ghrelin.2
Etiology
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:50 AM
AAOS | Diabetes Mellitus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003007
4/21

Type 1 diabetes mellitus is characterized by destruction of pancreatic beta cells, which most
frequently results from chronic inflammation secondary to an autoimmune process.
Type 2 diabetes mellitus is characterized by insulin resistance and relative insulin deficiency,
leading to chronic hyperglycemia.

Etiology
Type 1 diabetes mellitus is characterized by hyperglycemia and insulin deficiency
secondary to destruction of pancreatic beta cells, which most frequently results from
chronic inflammation secondary to an autoimmune process.3 Environmental factors
appear to lead to the development of type 1 diabetes mellitus in genetically susceptible
individuals. During a long period of latency, beta cells are destroyed increasingly;
however, patients maintain euglycemia and are asymptomatic.
Type 2 diabetes mellitus is characterized by insulin resistance and relative insulin
deficiency, which leads to chronic hyperglycemia. The complex development of type 2
diabetes mellitus is related to genetic and environmental risk factors. Patients with first-
degree relatives who have type 2 diabetes mellitus are at high risk for type 2 diabetes
mellitus.
Type 2 DM diabetes mellitus a stronger familial association than type 1 diabetes mellitus.
Environmental risk factors, namely obesity and a sedentary lifestyle, are strongly
implicated in the development of type 2 diabetes mellitus. Most patients with type 2
diabetes mellitus are obese. The connection between obesity and type 2 diabetes
mellitus is complex; however, it may occur via a combination of insulin resistance,
increased inflammation, deranged fatty acid metabolism, and mitochondrial
dysfunction.4
Natural History
Type 1 diabetes mellitus
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:50 AM
AAOS | Diabetes Mellitus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003007
5/21

Peak incidence occurs at age 10 to 14 years; however, type 1 diabetes mellitus also develops
with some frequency in adults.
Type 2 diabetes mellitus
Years before diagnosis, patients develop decreased insulin sensitivity, requiring increased
insulin secretion.
Beta cell function eventually may be lost because of so-called burnout.

Natural History
For patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus, genetic markers for susceptibility are present
from birth and have been identified in genome-wide association studies. After
autoimmunity develops, pancreatic beta cells are destroyed over time by autoantibodies;
however, months to years may pass before the condition can be diagnosed clinically. The
peak incidence of type 1 diabetes mellitus occurs in individuals aged 10 to 14 years.
Although type 1 diabetes mellitus historically has been known as juvenile diabetes, the
disease occurs in approximately 25% of adults.5
Patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus develop decreased insulin sensitivity years before
diagnosis, causing beta cells to increase insulin secretion to offset increased insulin
requirements.
Depending on the severity of disease, patients may lose beta cell function over a number
of years because of long-term insulin hypersecretion (so-called burnout of beta cells).
Risk Factors
Type 1 diabetes mellitus is an autoimmune disease and, therefore, few risk factors are
modifiable.
Type 2 diabetes mellitus has strong familial predisposition, and clear ties to obesity.

Risk Factors
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:50 AM
AAOS | Diabetes Mellitus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003007
6/21

Most patients who are diagnosed have additional risk factors related to lifestyle.
Approximately 90% of patients with diabetes mellitus are overweight (body mass index
>25 kg/m2) or obese (body mass index >30 kg/m2). Thirty-eight percent of patients are
physically inactive (<10 minutes of moderate to vigorous activity per week).
Tobacco is an additional risk factor; more than 20% of patients are tobacco users, and
approximately 40% of patients have a history of substantial tobacco use.1
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Type 1 diabetes mellitus
The classic presentation for type 1 diabetes mellitus is onset of polydipsia, polyuria, and
weight loss during childhood or adolescence.
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is another common presentation of type 1 diabetes mellitus and
is considered to be an emergency.
Type 2 diabetes mellitus
Most patients who are diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus are asymptomatic and are
diagnosed because of screening on routine laboratory workup.

Patient History
The classic presentation of type 1 diabetes mellitus is onset of polydipsia, polyuria, and
weight loss during childhood or adolescence. Polydipsia and polyuria are caused by
osmotic diuresis. After blood glucose levels are higher than 180 mg/dL, glucose spills into
the urine, resulting in osmotic diuresis and hypovolemia. Nocturnal enuresis also is
common among children with type 1 diabetes mellitus.6 Insulin deficiency leads to
breakdown of fat and muscle, which results in weight loss. Patients also report nausea
and loss of appetite, likely related to ketotic state.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:50 AM
AAOS | Diabetes Mellitus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003007
7/21

DKA, which is characterized by ketoacidosis and hyperglycemia, is another common
presentation of type 1 diabetes mellitus and is an emergency. Approximately 25% of
patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus initially present with DKA.
Most patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus are asymptomatic and are diagnosed
because of screening on routine laboratory workup. Similar to patients with type 1
diabetes mellitus, symptomatic patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus may present with
polydipsia, polyuria, and weight loss.
Occasionally, patients are diagnosed after more acute presentation—DKA or
hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS). HHS is characterized by severe hyperglycemia
but not ketoacidosis and occasionally is associated with symptoms of type 2 diabetes
mellitus. Rarely, patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus may present with DKA. Although
this is uncommon, providers should not assume that patients with DKA always have type
1 diabetes mellitus.
Physical Examination
Vital signs
Skin examination: acanthosis nigricans and lipodystrophy
Foot examination
Regular fundoscopic examination

Physical Examination
Physical examination should being with basics and vital signs—height, weight, body
mass index, and blood pressure. A careful physical examination should be performed.
Skin examination may reveal acanthosis nigricans—dark, velvety patches that classically
occur at the base of the neck but may be present in any body folds. Skin examination
also should include evaluation of injection sites for patients being treated with insulin to
ensure absence of lipodystrophy—abnormal fat distribution related to repeated insulin
injection.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:50 AM
AAOS | Diabetes Mellitus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003007
8/21

Foot examination should be performed regularly to evaluate for foot deformity or ulcers,
and patients should be screened for peripheral artery disease and for neuropathy via
monofilament examination.
Patients also should be referred to ophthalmology for a regular fundoscopic
examination to screen for retinopathy.
Laboratory Workup
Diabetes mellitus can be diagnosed if a patient has classic symptoms of hyperglycemic and a
random glucose level higher than or equal to 200 mg/dL.
If a patient is asymptomatic, a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus requires positive results on two of
the following tests (either two different tests on the same day or the same test on a
subsequent day):
Hemoglobin A1c level higher than or equal to 6.5%
Fasting plasma glucose level higher than or equal to 125 mg/dL
Two-hour oral glucose tolerance test higher than or equal to 200 mg/dL

Laboratory Workup
Diabetes mellitus can be diagnosed if a patient has classic hyperglycemic symptoms and
a random glucose level higher than or equal to 200 mg/dL. Most patients will be
diagnosed on routine screening by their primary care physician.
If a patient is asymptomatic, a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus requires positive results on
two of the following tests—either two different tests on the same day or the same test
on a subsequent day7:
Hemoglobin A1c level higher than or equal to 6.5%
Fasting plasma glucose level higher than or equal to 125 mg/dL
Two-hour oral glucose tolerance test higher than or equal to 200 mg/dL
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:50 AM
AAOS | Diabetes Mellitus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003007
9/21

A hemoglobin A1c test measures glycosylated hemoglobin and reflects mean blood
glucose level over the previous 2 to 3 months. An oral glucose tolerance test requires a
fasting patient to drink a solution containing 75 g of sugar and have blood drawn 2 hours
later.
If type 1 diabetes mellitus is suspected, the provider should assess antibodies (although
absence of antibodies does not rule out type 1 diabetes mellitus) and insulin and C-
peptide levels, which will provide information on endogenous insulin production.
Patients with diabetes mellitus should be tested annually for lipids, liver function, serum
creatinine levels, and ratio of urinary albumin to creatinine to identify complications or
factors that may increase cardiovascular risk.8
Monitoring
Patients with diabetes mellitus often require close monitoring of blood glucose to guide
management and avoid complications.
Blood glucose is commonly monitored via the following methods:
Hemoglobin A1c test
Blood glucose test (finger stick and glucometer)
Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) device
Frucosamine test

Monitoring
Several common methods are available for monitoring glycemic control. A hemoglobin
A1c test, blood glucose test (via finger sticks and a glucometer), and CGM device
measure glucose levels. A test for the biomarker frucosamine also is used to estimate
glycemic control; however, compared with the hemoglobin A1c test, it represents a
shorter period of mean glucose values (several weeks) and provides fewer clinical data.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:50 AM
AAOS | Diabetes Mellitus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003007
10/21

The frucosamine test is used much less frequently than the other tests, mostly in
patients with abnormal hemoglobin levels or unexpected hemoglobin A1c levels.
The type of diabetes mellitus and the severity of disease determine the need for
monitoring. For example, mild type 2 diabetes mellitus that is well controlled via a sole
oral agent may require only hemoglobin A1c level evaluation every 6 months.
Conversely, patients who are insulin dependent require close glucose monitoring and
often use a CGM.
Hemoglobin A1c levels generally are assessed every 3 to 6 months. Blood glucose levels
can be measured frequently at home via self-administered finger stick and can be read
via a glucometer. CGM devices are worn continuously, generally on the arm or abdomen.
They measure interstitial glucose levels and send frequent readings to a handheld device
or phone app. CGM devices are relatively new and are becoming increasingly popular
because they spare patients from the need to perform frequent finger sticks and provide
a large amount of data on blood glucose trends. Certain CGM models also can alert
patients to excursions in blood glucose levels, including hypoglycemia.
Outpatient Glycemic Targets
Targets for hemoglobin A1c levels may vary considerably based on patient demographics.
For most adults, a goal hemoglobin A1c level is less than 7%.

Outpatient Glycemic Targets
Targets for hemoglobin A1c levels may vary considerably based on patient
demographics.9 For most adults, a goal hemoglobin A1c level is less than 7%; however, a
stricter goal hemoglobin A1c level (<6.5%) is reasonable for patients who have a long life
expectancy, short duration of diabetes mellitus, or mild disease if they do not have
serious hypoglycemia. Other patients may require a looser goal hemoglobin A1c level
(<8%) if they have serious hypoglycemia, a limited life expectancy, or serious
comorbidities/complications. Ideally, women who are pregnant should aim for an
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:50 AM
AAOS | Diabetes Mellitus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003007
11/21

hemoglobin A1c level of less than 6%; however, this may be relaxed to less than 7% if
necessary to prevent serious hypoglycemia.
Inpatient Glycemic Targets
Patients who have multiple blood glucose levels higher than or equal to 180 mg/dL should be
treated for hyperglycemia.
A goal blood glucose level for most inpatients is 140 to 180 mg/dL

Inpatient Glycemic Targets
Patients who have multiple blood glucose levels higher than or equal to 180 mg/dL
should be treated for hyperglycemia regardless whether they have a known history of
diabetes mellitus because blood glucose levels elevated above this range are associated
with poor outcomes. A goal blood glucose level for most inpatients is 140 to 180 mg/dL.
Stricter targets (<140 mg/dL) generally are not associated with improved outcomes;
however, they may be appropriate in certain circumstances in patients without
substantial hypoglycemia.
Hemoglobin A1c levels should be obtained for inpatients with diabetes mellitus who
have not had their levels assessed in the previous 3 months.10
Management
Goals of Management
Management of diabetes mellitus aims to normalize blood glucose levels to attain goal
hemoglobin A1c and blood glucose levels.
Inpatient Therapy
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:50 AM
AAOS | Diabetes Mellitus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003007
12/21

Although patients are in the hospital, noninsulin agents generally are withheld.
Patients are treated with insulin to reach goal blood glucose levels. Insulin regimens
generally consist of a combination of basal and bolus insulin, even if the patient can take
nothing by mouth.
Patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus should never have insulin withheld because of a risk for
DKA.
Patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus who are being treated with insulin often require
decreased insulin doses in the hospital because their diet differs from that at home.

Inpatient Therapy
Although patients are in the hospital, noninsulin agents generally are withheld, and
patients are administered insulin to reach goal blood glucose levels. Insulin regimens
generally consist of a combination of basal and bolus insulin, even if the patient is
restricted to nothing by mouth. Blood glucose levels should be reviewed daily in the
hospital, and insulin should be titrated accordingly.
Patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus should never have insulin withheld because of the
risk for DKA. Their basal insulin should continuous; however, insulin doses can be
lowered if concern for hypoglycemia exists (ie, if patients are restricted to nothing by
mouth or have decreased intake by mouth). However, patients with type 1 diabetes
mellitus require at least 0.1 U/kg of long-acting insulin for basal needs.
Patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus being treated with insulin often require decreased
insulin doses in the hospital because of a different diet; it generally is preferable to
decrease doses by 25% to 50% rather than withholding insulin altogether, which
increases the risk for hyperglycemia.
As patients near hospital discharge, oral agents can be restarted. Metformin should not
be restarted in patients with ongoing renal issues or who require repeat surgery or
imaging with contrast.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:50 AM
AAOS | Diabetes Mellitus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003007
13/21

Types of Management
Management can be divided into two main categories: insulin therapies and noninsulin therapies.

Insulin Therapies
The goal of insulin therapy is to replicate physiologic production. For patients with type 1
diabetes mellitus, insulin is required from time of diagnosis because of lack of
endogenous production. Patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus need to receive regular
insulin injections to prevent DKA.
Patients require long- and short-acting insulin to cover their basal and bolus needs,
respectively. Long-acting insulin doses should never drop to less than 0.1 U/kg because
lower doses may not cover basal needs and may be associated with a risk of DKA.
A minority of patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (less than 10%) require insulin within
1 year of diagnosis; however, many patients will require insulin over time because of
beta cell burnout and increased insulin resistance.
Insulin generally is indicated in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus who have a
hemoglobin A1c level higher than 9% at time of diagnosis or in whom goal hemoglobin
A1c levels cannot be attained via noninsulin agents alone.
Many clinicians begin with a daily dose of basal insulin alone; however, patients with
type 2 diabetes mellitus who have considerable insulin resistance may require large
doses.
Insulin comes in many different formulations, with the primary differences being time of
onset, duration, and peak. Insulin concentration is expressed as units/mL; the most
common concentration is 100 U/mL (U100).
Basal (long-acting) insulins cover background physiologic needs for the entire day. The
most common basal insulin is U100 glargine, which acts over 24 hours and has no
appreciable peak.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:50 AM
AAOS | Diabetes Mellitus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003007
14/21

Short-acting insulins have a quick onset (15 minutes) and a short duration of action (3 to
5 hours) and are used to cover meals or correct hyperglycemic episodes quickly.
Formulations are aspart, lispro, and glulisine.
Regular insulin is the cheapest form and generally is used in insulin drips in the hospital.
Insulin also comes in a premixed form and is a combination of short and intermediate
insulins in a single shot, usually administered two times/day.
Insulin pumps are medical devices that continuously deliver insulin through a small port,
usually on the stomach or arm. Newer pumps may be small or even tubeless. The
pumps provide patients with basal insulin as an ongoing drip through the pump;
however, a bolus is required before meals or for correction if patients become
hyperglycemic.
If the insulin pump is removed for any reason (such as during surgery), the patient needs
to be transitioned to insulin injections, preferably 2 hours before removing the pump, to
ensure that the injection has time to work.

Noninsulin Therapies
Patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus should be encouraged to pursue lifestyle
modifications; some patients may be able to avoid pharmacotherapy altogether, and
other patients can reduce their need for medications. Lifestyle modifications include
nutrition therapy and increased physical activity.
A nutritionist can help patients monitor carbohydrate intake and achieve weight loss.
Patients should aim for at least 150 minutes per week of moderate physical activity. For
patients who use tobacco, smoking cessation is imperative.
For patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus who are not able to reach goal glycemic levels
via lifestyle modifications alone, oral agents are an appropriate choice. Oral agents
generally should not be used in patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:50 AM
AAOS | Diabetes Mellitus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003007
15/21

Metformin is the preferred initial therapy for most patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus.
Contraindications to metformin include a glomerular filtration rate of less than 30
mL/min, active liver disease, and a history of lactic acidosis with metformin. Metformin
should be withheld for 48 hours after imaging studies with contrast.
Multiple additional oral agents can be administered to patients who cannot tolerate
metformin or who require additional therapies to reach glycemic goals. Examples
include dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors (eg, sitagliptin, linagliptin), glucagonlike peptide-
1 receptor agonists (eg, liraglutide), sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (eg,
empagliflozin, canagliflozin), sulfonylureas (eg, glipizide, glyburide), and
thiazolidinediones (eg, pioglitazone).
Surgical Management
Pancreas transplant: relatively uncommon treatment option for diabetes mellitus

Surgical Management
Pancreas transplant rarely is performed to manage diabetes mellitus. Simultaneous
pancreas-kidney or pancreas after kidney transplants are the most commonly
performed pancreas transplants and are favored over pancreas transplant alone
because patients who undergo such procedures already are being treated via
immunosuppression for renal transplant. In general, qualifying patients have type 1
diabetes mellitus with end-stage renal disease.
Patients who are eligible for pancreas transplant alone have severe complications of
diabetes mellitus, incapacitating issues with insulin therapy, and failed to respond to
other treatment strategies.11 Islet transplant is an evolving technology that is restricted
to research studies at this time.
Complications
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:50 AM
AAOS | Diabetes Mellitus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003007
16/21

DKA or HHS: requires admission to an intensive care unit for insulin drip and close monitoring
Microvascular complications
Macrovascular complications
Musculoskeletal complications

Complications
DKA and HHS are emergencies that require admission to an intensive care unit for
insulin drip and close monitoring. The conditions may occur at the time of diagnosis of
diabetes mellitus, if insulin doses are missed, or in patients with other systemic illness
that may increase insulin needs.
Microvascular complications are common in patients with poorly controlled or
longstanding diabetes mellitus. Regular screening is required to diagnose and monitor
retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy.
Macrovascular complications also are quite common; atherosclerosis is considerably
increased in patients with diabetes mellitus. Many patients with diabetes mellitus are
candidates for aspirin and statins, and blood pressure levels and lipids should be closely
monitored.
Numerous musculoskeletal diseases, including carpal tunnel syndrome, Dupuytren
disease, adhesive capsulitis, neuropathic arthropathy, and diabetic muscle infarction are
common.
Diabetic foot ulcers may occur in as many one-fourth of patients with diabetes mellitus
over the course of their life. Numerous risk factors include neuropathy, foot deformity,
peripheral artery disease, infection, and impaired healing.12 Monofilament testing can
be performed to detect diabetic neuropathy.
Perioperative Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:50 AM
AAOS | Diabetes Mellitus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6003007
17/21

Diabetes mellitus is associated with an increased risk for perioperative complications,
particularly increased rates of infection.
Glycemic targets should be addressed aggressively in the perioperative period.
Intraoperative steroids
Insulin pumps

Perioperative Management
Patients with diabetes mellitus have higher rates of surgical complications because of
elevated cardiovascular risk and predisposition for infections. In patients who are
undergoing elective procedures, glycemic control should be targeted. Although a
hemoglobin A1c level 7% may be difficult to attain in many patients, some physicians or
hospitals have set arbitrary cutoffs for hemoglobin A1c levels at approximately 8% to
limit complications in patients with very poor glycemic control and to encourage patients
to aggressively manage their diabetes mellitus preoperatively.13
Postoperatively, a blood glucose level higher than 200 mg/dL is a risk factor for surgical
site infection in orthopaedic patients. In all surgical patients, tight perioperative glycemic
control decreases rates of complications, including bacteremia, pneumonia, acute kidney
injury, and respiratory failure.
Steroids increase blood glucose levels, and those who are being treated with
intraoperative steroids may have increased blood glucose levels, potentially
necessitating additional insulin. Blood glucose levels should be monitored carefully in
these patients to prevent hyperglycemia for the duration of steroid use. Patients who are
not being treated with steroids may experience elevated cortisol related to the stress of
surgery, which may lead to marked hyperglycemia.14
In patients being treated with insulin pumps preoperatively, these devices are being
increasingly used during surgical procedures, particularly those of short duration, or are
being restarted quickly postoperatively. Glycemic control should be closely monitored by
the anesthesiologist intraoperatively, and, in patients with hypoglycemia, the pump
